BACKGROUND
Abiraterone acetate, a drug that blocks endogenous androgen synthesis, plus predni-
sone is indicated for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. We evaluated the
clinical benefit of abiraterone acetate plus prednisone with androgen-deprivation ther
apy in patients with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer.
METHODS
In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 1199 pa-
tients to receive either androgen-deprivation therapy plus abiraterone acetate (1000 mg
daily, given once daily as four 250-mg tablets) plus prednisone (5 mg daily) (the
abiraterone group) or androgen-deprivation therapy plus dual placebos (the placebo
group). The two primary end points were overall survival and radiographic progression-
free survival.
RESULTS
After a median follow-up of 30.4 months at a planned interim analysis (after 406 pa-
tients had died), the median overall survival was significantly longer in the abiraterone
group than in the placebo group (not reached vs. 34.7 months) (hazard ratio for death,
0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The median length of radio-
graphic progression-free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone group and 14.8
months in the placebo group (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.47; 95%
CI, 0.39 to 0.55; P<0.001). Significantly better outcomes in all secondary end points
were observed in the abiraterone group, including the time until pain progression, next
subsequent therapy for prostate cancer, initiation of chemotherapy, and prostate-
specific antigen progression (P<0.001 for all comparisons), along with next symptom-
atic skeletal events (P = 0.009). These findings led to the unanimous recommendation
by the independent data and safety monitoring committee that the trial be unblinded
and crossover be allowed for patients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone. Rates
of grade 3 hypertension and hypokalemia were higher in the abiraterone group.
CONCLUSIONS
The addition of abiraterone acetate and prednisone to androgen-deprivation therapy
significantly increased overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival in
men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer. (Funded
by Janssen Research and Development; LATITUDE ClinicalTrials.gov number,
NCT01715285.)

etastatic, castration-sensitive
prostate cancer accounts for approxi-
mately 3% of all new prostate-cancer
diagnoses in the United States.1 Historically,
androgen-deprivation therapy consisting of bilat-
eral orchiectomy or luteinizing hormone-releas-
ing hormone analogues, with or without first-
generation androgen-receptor inhibitors, has been
the standard of care.2 Although the majority of
patients have an initial response to androgen-
deprivation therapy, most men with metastases
have progression to castration-resistant prostate
cancer within a median of approximately 1 year.3-5
Resistance to androgen-deprivation therapy is
largely driven by the reactivation of androgen-
receptor signaling through persistent adrenal an-
drogen production, up-regulation of intratumoral
testosterone production, modification of the bi-
ologic characteristics of androgen receptors, and
steroidogenic parallel pathways.2
The clinical benefit of adding docetaxel to
androgen-deprivation therapy versus treatment
with androgen-deprivation therapy alone has been
shown in three randomized, phase 3 trials -
Chemohormonal Therapy Versus Androgen Ab-
lation Randomized Trial for Extensive Disease in
Prostate Cancer (CHAARTED),5,6 Systemic Ther-
apy in Advancing or Metastatic Prostate Cancer:
Evaluation of Drug Efficacy (STAMPEDE),7 and
GETUG-153,8 - which collectively included more
than 3000 men with metastatic, castration-sensi-
tive prostate cancer. Androgen-deprivation ther-
apy plus docetaxel is now a standard of care for
men with metastatic, castration-sensitive pros-
tate cancer who are eligible for chemotherapy,
particularly those with a high metastatic burden,
as defined in the respective studies.9-11 Barriers
to the use of docetaxel include advanced patient
age, poor performance status, coexisting illness-
es, and patient preferences.9,12 Retrospective analy-
ses exploring real-world practice patterns13,14 indi-
cate that men with newly diagnosed, metastatic,
castration-sensitive prostate cancer who are not
being treated in clinical trials may be nearly a
decade older than those treated in clinical trials.
The concern with respect to chemotherapy-related
toxicity and the effect of coexisting illnesses on
complications is based on the severity of the
toxicity that has been observed. Chemotherapy-
related deaths were documented in all three
randomized trials in which docetaxel was added
to androgen-deprivation therapy.3,5,7
Abiraterone acetate, the prodrug of abiraterone,
inhibits cytochrome P-450c17, a critical enzyme
in androgen biosynthesis.15,16 Recent studies im-
plicate its active D4A metabolite in antitumor
effects, presumably through blockade of multi-
ple steroidogenic enzymes and antagonism of the
androgen receptor.17 Abiraterone acetate (here-
after referred to as abiraterone) in combination
with prednisone has been shown to significantly
increase overall survival and provide additional
clinical benefits in patients with metastatic,
castration-resistant prostate cancer who have
not received chemotherapy and in those who
have received previous docetaxel.18-22 The combi-
nation of abiraterone plus prednisone and andro-
gen-deprivation therapy has been shown to reduce
tumor burden in men with high-risk, localized
prostate cancer who are receiving neoadjuvant
therapy, which suggests a potential role for
inhibiting extragonadal androgen biosynthesis
before the emergence of castration resistance in
men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-
sensitive prostate cancer.23,24 In LATITUDE, a
multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-
controlled, phase 3 trial, we evaluated the addition
of abiraterone plus prednisone to androgen-
deprivation therapy, as compared with androgen-
deprivation therapy and dual placebos, on overall
survival, radiographic progression-free survival,
and clinically relevant measures in men with
newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive
prostate cancer.

Harmonisation Good Clinical Practice Guide-

consent.

38|BACKGROUND
39|Abiraterone acetate, a drug that blocks endogenous androgen synthesis, plus predni-
40|sone is indicated for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. We evaluated the
41|clinical benefit of abiraterone acetate plus prednisone with androgen-deprivation ther
42|apy in patients with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer.
43|METHODS
44|In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 1199 pa-
45|tients to receive either androgen-deprivation therapy plus abiraterone acetate (1000 mg
46|daily, given once daily as four 250-mg tablets) plus prednisone (5 mg daily) (the
47|abiraterone group) or androgen-deprivation therapy plus dual placebos (the placebo
48|group). The two primary end points were overall survival and radiographic progression-
49|free survival.
50|RESULTS
51|After a median follow-up of 30.4 months at a planned interim analysis (after 406 pa-
52|tients had died), the median overall survival was significantly longer in the abiraterone
53|group than in the placebo group (not reached vs. 34.7 months) (hazard ratio for death,
54|0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The median length of radio-
55|graphic progression-free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone group and 14.8
56|months in the placebo group (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.47; 95%
57|CI, 0.39 to 0.55; P<0.001). Significantly better outcomes in all secondary end points
58|were observed in the abiraterone group, including the time until pain progression, next
59|subsequent therapy for prostate cancer, initiation of chemotherapy, and prostate-
60|specific antigen progression (P<0.001 for all comparisons), along with next symptom-
61|atic skeletal events (P = 0.009). These findings led to the unanimous recommendation
62|by the independent data and safety monitoring committee that the trial be unblinded
63|and crossover be allowed for patients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone. Rates
64|of grade 3 hypertension and hypokalemia were higher in the abiraterone group.
65|CONCLUSIONS
66|The addition of abiraterone acetate and prednisone to androgen-deprivation therapy
67|significantly increased overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival in
68|men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer. (Funded
69|by Janssen Research and Development; LATITUDE ClinicalTrials.gov number,
70|NCT01715285.)

5|etastatic, castration-sensitive
6|prostate cancer accounts for approxi-
7|mately 3% of all new prostate-cancer
8|diagnoses in the United States.1 Historically,
9|androgen-deprivation therapy consisting of bilat-
10|eral orchiectomy or luteinizing hormone-releas-
11|ing hormone analogues, with or without first-
12|generation androgen-receptor inhibitors, has been
13|the standard of care.2 Although the majority of
14|patients have an initial response to androgen-
15|deprivation therapy, most men with metastases
16|have progression to castration-resistant prostate
17|cancer within a median of approximately 1 year.3-5
18|Resistance to androgen-deprivation therapy is
19|largely driven by the reactivation of androgen-
20|receptor signaling through persistent adrenal an-
21|drogen production, up-regulation of intratumoral
22|testosterone production, modification of the bi-
23|ologic characteristics of androgen receptors, and
24|steroidogenic parallel pathways.2
25|The clinical benefit of adding docetaxel to
26|androgen-deprivation therapy versus treatment
27|with androgen-deprivation therapy alone has been
28|shown in three randomized, phase 3 trials -
29|Chemohormonal Therapy Versus Androgen Ab-
30|lation Randomized Trial for Extensive Disease in
31|Prostate Cancer (CHAARTED),5,6 Systemic Ther-
32|apy in Advancing or Metastatic Prostate Cancer:
33|Evaluation of Drug Efficacy (STAMPEDE),7 and
34|GETUG-153,8 - which collectively included more
35|than 3000 men with metastatic, castration-sensi-
36|tive prostate cancer. Androgen-deprivation ther-
37|apy plus docetaxel is now a standard of care for
38|men with metastatic, castration-sensitive pros-
39|tate cancer who are eligible for chemotherapy,
40|particularly those with a high metastatic burden,
41|as defined in the respective studies.9-11 Barriers
42|to the use of docetaxel include advanced patient
43|age, poor performance status, coexisting illness-
44|es, and patient preferences.9,12 Retrospective analy-
45|ses exploring real-world practice patterns13,14 indi-
46|cate that men with newly diagnosed, metastatic,
47|castration-sensitive prostate cancer who are not
48|being treated in clinical trials may be nearly a
49|decade older than those treated in clinical trials.
50|The concern with respect to chemotherapy-related
51|toxicity and the effect of coexisting illnesses on
52|complications is based on the severity of the
53|toxicity that has been observed. Chemotherapy-
54|related deaths were documented in all three
55|randomized trials in which docetaxel was added
56|to androgen-deprivation therapy.3,5,7
57|Abiraterone acetate, the prodrug of abiraterone,
58|inhibits cytochrome P-450c17, a critical enzyme
59|in androgen biosynthesis.15,16 Recent studies im-
60|plicate its active D4A metabolite in antitumor
61|effects, presumably through blockade of multi-
62|ple steroidogenic enzymes and antagonism of the
63|androgen receptor.17 Abiraterone acetate (here-
64|after referred to as abiraterone) in combination
65|with prednisone has been shown to significantly
66|increase overall survival and provide additional
67|clinical benefits in patients with metastatic,
68|castration-resistant prostate cancer who have
69|not received chemotherapy and in those who
70|have received previous docetaxel.18-22 The combi-
71|nation of abiraterone plus prednisone and andro-
72|gen-deprivation therapy has been shown to reduce
73|tumor burden in men with high-risk, localized
74|prostate cancer who are receiving neoadjuvant
75|therapy, which suggests a potential role for
76|inhibiting extragonadal androgen biosynthesis
77|before the emergence of castration resistance in
78|men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-
79|sensitive prostate cancer.23,24 In LATITUDE, a
80|multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-
81|controlled, phase 3 trial, we evaluated the addition
82|of abiraterone plus prednisone to androgen-
83|deprivation therapy, as compared with androgen-
84|deprivation therapy and dual placebos, on overall
85|survival, radiographic progression-free survival,
86|and clinically relevant measures in men with
87|newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive
88|prostate cancer.
89|Methods
90|Trial Design and Conduct
91|The trial was conducted at 235 sites in 34 coun-
92|tries in Europe, the Asia-Pacific region, Latin
93|America, and Canada. The trial protocol (avail-
94|able with the full text of this article at NEJM.org)
95|was approved by the review board at each par-
96|ticipating institution. The trial was conducted
97|according to the principles of the Declaration of
98|Helsinki and the International Conference on
99|Harmonisation Good Clinical Practice Guide-
100|lines. All the patients provided written informed
101|consent.
102|An independent data and safety monitoring
103|committee was commissioned by the sponsor,
104|Janssen Research and Development, to review
105|safety data on a regular basis and review effi-
106|cacy data at planned interim analyses. The trial

73|The two primary efficacy end points were overall

BACKGROUND
Abiraterone acetate, a drug that blocks endogenous androgen synthesis, plus predni-
sone is indicated for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. We evaluated the
clinical benefit of abiraterone acetate plus prednisone with androgen-deprivation ther
apy in patients with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer.
METHODS
In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, we randomly assigned 1199 pa-
tients to receive either androgen-deprivation therapy plus abiraterone acetate (1000 mg
daily, given once daily as four 250-mg tablets) plus prednisone (5 mg daily) (the
abiraterone group) or androgen-deprivation therapy plus dual placebos (the placebo
group). The two primary end points were overall survival and radiographic progression-
free survival.
RESULTS
After a median follow-up of 30.4 months at a planned interim analysis (after 406 pa-
tients had died), the median overall survival was significantly longer in the abiraterone
group than in the placebo group (not reached vs. 34.7 months) (hazard ratio for death,
0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.51 to 0.76; P<0.001). The median length of radio-
graphic progression-free survival was 33.0 months in the abiraterone group and 14.8
months in the placebo group (hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.47; 95%
CI, 0.39 to 0.55; P<0.001). Significantly better outcomes in all secondary end points
were observed in the abiraterone group, including the time until pain progression, next
subsequent therapy for prostate cancer, initiation of chemotherapy, and prostate-
specific antigen progression (P<0.001 for all comparisons), along with next symptom-
atic skeletal events (P = 0.009). These findings led to the unanimous recommendation
by the independent data and safety monitoring committee that the trial be unblinded
and crossover be allowed for patients in the placebo group to receive abiraterone. Rates
of grade 3 hypertension and hypokalemia were higher in the abiraterone group.
CONCLUSIONS
The addition of abiraterone acetate and prednisone to androgen-deprivation therapy
significantly increased overall survival and radiographic progression-free survival in
men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-sensitive prostate cancer. (Funded

prostate cancer accounts for approxi-
mately 3% of all new prostate-cancer
diagnoses in the United States.1 Historically,
androgen-deprivation therapy consisting of bilat-
eral orchiectomy or luteinizing hormone-releas-
ing hormone analogues, with or without first-
generation androgen-receptor inhibitors, has been
the standard of care.2 Although the majority of
patients have an initial response to androgen-
deprivation therapy, most men with metastases
have progression to castration-resistant prostate
cancer within a median of approximately 1 year.3-5
Resistance to androgen-deprivation therapy is
largely driven by the reactivation of androgen-
receptor signaling through persistent adrenal an-
drogen production, up-regulation of intratumoral
testosterone production, modification of the bi-
ologic characteristics of androgen receptors, and
steroidogenic parallel pathways.2
The clinical benefit of adding docetaxel to
androgen-deprivation therapy versus treatment
with androgen-deprivation therapy alone has been
shown in three randomized, phase 3 trials -
Chemohormonal Therapy Versus Androgen Ab-
lation Randomized Trial for Extensive Disease in
Prostate Cancer (CHAARTED),5,6 Systemic Ther-
apy in Advancing or Metastatic Prostate Cancer:
Evaluation of Drug Efficacy (STAMPEDE),7 and
GETUG-153,8 - which collectively included more
than 3000 men with metastatic, castration-sensi-
tive prostate cancer. Androgen-deprivation ther-
apy plus docetaxel is now a standard of care for
men with metastatic, castration-sensitive pros-
tate cancer who are eligible for chemotherapy,
particularly those with a high metastatic burden,
as defined in the respective studies.9-11 Barriers
to the use of docetaxel include advanced patient
age, poor performance status, coexisting illness-
es, and patient preferences.9,12 Retrospective analy-
ses exploring real-world practice patterns13,14 indi-
cate that men with newly diagnosed, metastatic,
castration-sensitive prostate cancer who are not
being treated in clinical trials may be nearly a
decade older than those treated in clinical trials.
The concern with respect to chemotherapy-related
toxicity and the effect of coexisting illnesses on
complications is based on the severity of the
toxicity that has been observed. Chemotherapy-
related deaths were documented in all three
randomized trials in which docetaxel was added
to androgen-deprivation therapy.3,5,7
Abiraterone acetate, the prodrug of abiraterone,
inhibits cytochrome P-450c17, a critical enzyme
in androgen biosynthesis.15,16 Recent studies im-

effects, presumably through blockade of multi-

androgen receptor.17 Abiraterone acetate (here-
after referred to as abiraterone) in combination
with prednisone has been shown to significantly
increase overall survival and provide additional
clinical benefits in patients with metastatic,
castration-resistant prostate cancer who have
not received chemotherapy and in those who
have received previous docetaxel.18-22 The combi-
nation of abiraterone plus prednisone and andro-

tumor burden in men with high-risk, localized
prostate cancer who are receiving neoadjuvant
therapy, which suggests a potential role for
inhibiting extragonadal androgen biosynthesis
before the emergence of castration resistance in
men with newly diagnosed, metastatic, castration-

3.5
Analysis of Efficacy Endpoints
Analysis of efficacy endpoints will be conducted on the ITT Population. The primary analysis
on the primary and secondary efficacy endpoints will be based on the stratified log rank test;
sensitivity analyses using non-stratified log rank test and Cox proportional hazards model will
also be performed as supportive analyses.
3.5.1
Efficacy Analysis for the Primary Endpoint of rPFS
The efficacy endpoint of rPFS is defined in Section 1.3.1.1. The rPFS distribution and median
rPFS and the 95% confidence interval will be estimated using Kaplan-Meier method. Note that
statistical inference of rPFS will not be conducted in the context of group sequential testing
design. The following SAS® code will be used for the analysis:
proc lifetest data=DATASET_NAME;
(1)
time rPFSTIME*CENSOR(0);
strata ECOG VISCERAL
group=TREATMENT;
run;
where DATASET_NAME is the name of the dataset, rPFSTIME is a vector containing the OS
measurement for each patient, CENSOR is its respective censoring vector, TREATMENT is a
vector containing treatment group assignment, and ECOG and VISCERAL are vectors for the
stratification factors of ECOG PS score category and visceral status at baseline.
The resulting statistic (stratified log rank test statistic) will be evaluated using East® to ensure
that it is compared with the appropriate stopping boundary given the precise number of events
observed at the time of the interim analysis. If the statistic crosses a stopping boundary, then the
p value from the SAS® output will be used.
Supportive analysis using the Cox proportional hazards model will also be performed. The score
statistic (which is equivalent to log rank test statistic) may be used to provide an adjusted
estimate of the HR and corresponding 2-tailed 95% confidence interval. This information will
be included in the IDMC package for review as detailed in the IDMC charter.
